7 Things to Know Before Visiting Sumba, Indonesia’s Quiet Island 

by Heather Leave a Comment
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:35
Instaread

You type “Sumba” into a flight search, and the first result is Sumbawa Besar. Plenty of travellers have clicked it without a second look and ended up on the wrong island. That small slip says a lot about Sumba. It sits off most people’s radar, and the trip goes far better for anyone who does a little homework first. 

1. Is Sumba the same as Sumbawa?

No. Sumba lies in the eastern half of Nusa Tenggara, south of Flores. Sumbawa is a separate island to the west. Check the airport code before paying for anything. 

The other surprise is scale. Sumba covers about 10,909.55 square kilometres, roughly the size of Jamaica or the island of Hawaii. That’s too much ground for a long weekend, and driving between the east and west ends eats into the day faster than the map suggests. Pick one end as a base, or plan a single move partway through. 

2. What is tourism like on Sumba? 

Very basic, outside a handful of resorts. Those resorts are polished and self-contained. Beyond their gates, guesthouses, signage and tourist services thin out quickly. Independent travel here suits the hardy: people comfortable with patchy information, simple rooms and plans that shift by the hour. 

That rawness is the draw for some visitors. Others find it exhausting by day three, so be honest about which camp you’re in before booking a week of backpacking. 

3. Should you see Flores first? 

For a first trip east of Bali, yes. 

One assessment puts Sumba roughly ten years behind Flores in tourism maturity, and another says fifteen. Either way, Flores has more transport, more guides and more places to stay, which makes it a gentler introduction to Nusa Tenggara. Get a feel for the region there. When you come to Sumba afterwards, slower and rougher travel won’t catch you off guard, and the island’s quiet will feel like a reward instead of a shock. 

4. How do you get to Sumba? 

Two airports serve the island: Tambolaka (TMC) in the west and Waingapu (WGP) in the east. Both have direct flights from several eastern Indonesian cities. Bali is the easiest jumping-off point, with a little over 20 flights a week to Tambolaka. 

That Bali connection makes it easy to fold Sumba into a wider trip. Well-planned Indonesia luxury tours tend to use it this way, pairing a few days among Bali’s rice terraces and beaches with the short hop east, so the island arrives as a natural next chapter. The flight is brief, and landing at Tambolaka lets you settle into a western base by the first afternoon. 

The slower route is by sea. The PELNI ship Awu calls at Waingapu twice on its 14-day round trip of Nusa Tenggara, and it’s described as the safest and best way to reach Sumba by water. It’s a good fit if you have time to spare and like the idea of arriving by ship. Confirm the schedule close to departure, since it can change. 

5. Can you use Grab or taxis on Sumba? 

No. There are no conventional taxis, and Grab and Gojek don’t operate on the island. Ojeks (motorbike taxis) wait around Waingapu and Tambolaka for short trips, which is handy for a market run and not much else. 

For anything beyond town, sort out transport in advance. A car with a driver arranged through your hotel or guesthouse is the most dependable setup. Booking it before you land saves a stressful first hour at the airport. 

6. Is it safe to ride a motorbike on Sumba? 

Not for first-timers. Roads are narrow and unpaved in places, they’re unlit after dark, and phone signal disappears across long stretches. A flat tyre at dusk with no reception is a miserable combination. If you want the freedom of a scooter, Bali is the place for it. On Sumba, a driver is worth the money.

7. When is the best time to visit Sumba? 

Go between May and November, during the dry season. The rainy season runs from December to April. On roads that are already rough, wet months make getting around slower and harder to predict. 

Before you book: 

  • Confirm your flight lands at Tambolaka (TMC) or Waingapu (WGP), not Sumbawa 
  • Set your dates between May and November 
  • Choose one end of the island as your main base 
  • Arrange a car and driver before arrival 
  • Download offline maps, since signal is patchy 
  • Consider a trip to Flores first if this is your first visit to the region
